strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: adapting web agents to new environments without human-annotated tasks, avoiding the test-set-leakage practices of some prior work.

The dual refinement design (task refinement during trajectory collection plus post-hoc trajectory refinement) is clearly motivated, and the analysis of why Explorer's continuous refinement fails (frequent task-intent changes, 68.3% budget-exceeding trajectories vs 6.3%) is a useful empirical insight.

Consistent empirical gains over multiple reimplemented baselines (Self-Instruct, OS-Genesis, Explorer) across two open-source agents, with a substantial overall improvement (e.g., 13.27 -> 20.80 for Qwen2.5-VL), and reasonable closeness to the test-set SFT upper bound.

Good analysis sections: ablations isolating categorized exploration vs. task refinement vs. trajectory refinement, data-quality statistics, trajectory completion/cost comparison (Table 3), t-SNE diversity visualization, and a data-scaling study.
Reasonable reproducibility support: WebArena Docker environments, shared LLM (GPT-4.1), budgets, hyperparameters, and full prompt templates in the appendix; code release promised.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (WebArena) and a subsampled 226-task evaluation set; generalization of the claims beyond this environment is untested, and no other domains (e.g., WebShop, Mind2Web, live sites) are considered despite the paper's framing about 'new websites'.

Data-quality metrics in Table 2 (task quality, trajectory quality, diversity) are judged by GPT-4.1 — the same model used for synthesis and refinement — creating a self-evaluation bias that plausibly favors SynthAgent; no human evaluation or independent judge corroborates these quality scores.

No variance reporting or significance testing: results are single runs on small per-site task counts (e.g., 26 tasks for CMS), and some per-site or ablation differences (e.g., +TR yielding +0.88 overall, or UI-TARS gaps of ~3 points) could be within noise.

Trajectory refinement edits trajectories offline (remove/reorder) without re-verification in the environment, so 'refined' trajectories may contain state-inconsistent transitions; the paper provides no validation that edited trajectories remain executable, which somewhat undercuts the 'high-quality supervision' claim.

Baseline comparisons raise concerns: Explorer's reimplementation performs drastically worse than the base model (4.44/4.96), and the authors attribute this to incompatibility with authenticated sites — plausible, but it means the strongest competitor is effectively not competitively deployed, weakening the headline comparison.

Novelty is incremental: the framework largely combines OS-Genesis-style reverse task synthesis and Explorer-style refinement with a categorization heuristic and LLM-based filtering/editing; the formal trigger predicate C in Eq. 1 is mostly cosmetic, as implementation is plain LLM prompting (Table 10).

The 'fully synthetic, no human involvement' claim still relies heavily on GPT-4.1 for exploration, task generation, refinement, and trajectory collection; the contribution is closer to closed-model distillation with quality filtering than fully autonomous adaptation.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and relevant problem—adapting web agents to new environments without human-annotated environment-specific data—and clearly positions itself against recent synthetic-data baselines (OS-Genesis, Explorer, Self-Instruct).

The proposed pipeline is concretely specified: categorized element exploration for task synthesis, trigger-based task refinement during collection (Eq. 1), and conservative post-hoc trajectory edits (remove/reorder/drop/keep). All prompts are provided in the appendix, which supports reproducibility of the method.

Evaluation is reasonably comprehensive for the setting: two open-source agent models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B), five WebArena websites, re-implemented baselines under a shared LLM (GPT-4.1), prompt template, and action space, plus an ablation (Table 4), data-scaling analysis (Fig. 4), and cost analysis (Table 3).

The empirical story is internally consistent: the same relative ordering of methods holds across both base models and most websites, and the ablation isolates the contribution of categorized exploration vs. task refinement vs. trajectory refinement.

The diagnostic analysis of why Explorer underperforms (task intent drift, 68.3% budget exceedance; authentication-heavy sites) is a useful negative result that is quantified rather than merely asserted.
weaknesses: All quality and diversity metrics in Tables 2, 3, and 5.1 are produced by GPT-4.1 as LLM-as-judge—but GPT-4.1 is also the model used for synthesis and refinement. This creates a circularity risk: the judge may favor outputs in its own style, and no human verification of any judged scores (task quality, trajectory quality, diversity, completion rates) is reported.

Only a single testbed (WebArena, and only a 226-task subset) is used. Claims about adapting agents to 'new environments' are not validated on any other benchmark (e.g., WebShop, Mind2Web, OSWorld), and the subset selection (one task per template, excluding cross-website tasks) limits generality of the conclusions.

No variance reporting: results are single runs, and several per-website eval sets are small (e.g., 26 CMS tasks), so differences of a few points (e.g., +OS-Genesis 14.60 vs. +Ours 17.26 for UI-TARS) may not be statistically meaningful. No significance tests or seeds are given.

The ablation is somewhat confusing: Table 4 shows +TR degrading Shopping and CMS relative to +CE (20.00→18.18, 14.04→12.28), which is only briefly acknowledged; the narrative 'marginal 0.88 improvement' obscures this non-monotonicity and the interaction between components deserves clearer analysis.

The A.1 evaluation setup (226 tasks, one per template) and the SFT upper bound (full 812 tasks, including evaluation tasks) are appropriately disclosed, but the smaller eval subset weakens precision, and the use of the full 812-task set for the upper bound makes the 'gap to upper bound' comparison in Section 4.2 not strictly comparable in data quantity.

Novelty is incremental: categorized exploration and dual (task+trajectory) refinement are reasonable engineering contributions on top of OS-Genesis/Explorer-style reverse task synthesis, and Table 8's task-generation prompt is largely adopted from OS-Genesis. The paper's contribution is mostly a system refinement rather than a new technique.

Code is only promised ('will be publicly available'); no artifact is verifiable at review time. Combined with GPT-4.1 dependence, full reproduction would incur nontrivial API costs without released data or code.

Writing has clarity issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('when detect a conflict', 'more clean and suitable one', 'SynthAgent only costs only about 60%'), and the method section relies heavily on qualitative description of refinement principles whose behavior could be better characterized (e.g., distribution of edit types applied, how often tasks were refined and by how much).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: quality control (hallucinated tasks, noisy trajectories) in fully synthetic supervision for web agent adaptation, and the dual-refinement design is a sensible, well-motivated decomposition of the problem.

The method is clearly specified: the task-refinement trigger predicate (Eq. 1) is concrete, the trajectory refinement edits (Remove/Reorder/Drop/Keep) are conservative and grounded, and the categorized exploration with a URL pool is a plausible fix for the inefficiency of random exploration in OS-Genesis.

The experimental design is generally careful: all baselines are reimplemented with the same LLM (GPT-4.1) and prompt/action space, two open-source agent backbones (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B) are evaluated, and a component-wise ablation (SS → CE → TR → JR) isolates each contribution, showing trajectory refinement is the key driver (+~4 points).

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: trajectory completion rates (Table 3) explain *why* Explorer underperforms (68.3% budget overruns), the t-SNE diversity analysis qualitatively supports the diversity claims, and a data-scaling curve (Figure 4) probes scalability. Per-trajectory API cost is also reported.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: WebArena's Docker deployment, an evaluation subset of 226 tasks with per-site counts, and full prompts in the appendix (Tables 7–12); code release is promised.
weaknesses: All data-quality, diversity, and completion metrics are judged by GPT-4.1 — the same model used for synthesis and refinement. This creates a circularity/bias risk (the judge may favor outputs from its own refinement pipeline), and there is no human validation of any judged metric, so the central 'quality improvement' claims rest on a single, potentially self-interested evaluator.

Evidence is limited to a single benchmark (WebArena) and a reduced 226-task evaluation subset; the claimed benefit of 'adapting to new environments' is never tested on a second environment family (e.g., WebShop, Mind2Web-live, or a real website), leaving generalization claims under-supported.

No statistical rigor: success rates are reported from what appears to be single runs, with no seeds, variance, or significance testing — notable given WebArena's small per-site task counts (e.g., 26 CMS tasks) and margins of a few points between SynthAgent and OS-Genesis on some sites (e.g., UI-TARS: 17.26 vs 14.60 overall).

The comparison to the SFT upper bound is not apples-to-apples (812 test-set tasks vs. 500 synthetic pairs), and Explorer's poor performance is partly attributed to a mismatch with authenticated websites acknowledged in the original paper; the reimplemented baseline may therefore be weaker than its original setting.

Novelty is incremental: the framework combines ideas already present in OS-Genesis (reverse task synthesis from exploration), Explorer (task refinement during collection), and trajectory filtering common in agent data curation; the categorized exploration is a relatively lightweight heuristic. The contribution is more of a careful engineering synthesis than a new technique.

Several method details are under-specified or potentially fragile: how 'ExistsUI'/'MissingArgs' are actually operationalized (LLM-prompted or programmatic?), how 'locally commutable' swaps are verified to preserve executable validity without re-execution, and how refined trajectories that delete/retain 'none' summary steps remain consistent with the final task answer.

The step budget (30), 500-pair dataset size, and 3-step history window are fixed choices whose sensitivity is not examined; the scaling analysis stops at 500 tasks/website, so it is unclear whether quality holds at larger scale.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies a genuine design tension in synthetic data generation for web agents (environment grounding improves task feasibility but trajectory grounding during execution introduces noise), and the dual-refinement design follows coherently from this analysis.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: two benchmarks (WebArena and Online-Mind2Web), three baselines re-implemented under a controlled setting (same synthesis LLM, same prompts/action space), ablations of all three proposed components (categorized exploration, task refinement, trajectory refinement), a data-scaling analysis, and a generalization test on unseen live websites.

Consistent and substantial empirical gains: SynthAgent outperforms all synthetic-data baselines on WebArena for both Qwen2.5-VL and UI-TARS backbones (+5-7 points over the strongest baselines), and generalizes to Online-Mind2Web without site-specific synthesis, approaching GPT-4.1 performance.

Strong reproducibility practices: code is stated to be publicly available, detailed implementation settings are provided (step budgets, context windows, learning rates, task counts per site), all prompt templates are included in the appendix, and multi-judge data quality evaluation (GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, Qwen3-30B) reduces dependence on a single evaluator.

Candid analysis of failure modes: the paper transparently investigates why Explorer underperforms (68.3% budget exceedance due to continuous refinement), verifies this matches the algorithmic design rather than an implementation error, and includes a head-to-head win-rate study of the reorder operation.
weaknesses: Potential circularity and bias in quality assessment: GPT-4.1 is used for synthesis, refinement, and (with GPT-5.1/Qwen3-30B) for data-quality judging; there is no human evaluation of synthetic task or trajectory quality, so the 'high-quality' claim rests largely on LLM judgments of LLM-generated data.

The task-refinement design risks trivializing tasks: the refinement prompt instructs that a refined task be 'either already completed or highly likely to complete within the next 1-2 steps', which could yield systematically easier tasks and inflate trajectory completion statistics (96.5% vs Explorer's 30.5%) without the refined tasks reflecting genuinely hard user intents; the paper does not measure task difficulty of refined tasks.

No variance or significance reporting: main results appear to be single runs; WebArena success rates are small absolute numbers where several-point differences could be sensitive to environment nondeterminism and decoding stochasticity, yet no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are given.

The conflict predicate C in Eq. 1 is presented as a lightweight, rule-like check (ExistsUI, MissingArgs, Stall), but the practical implementation of MissingArgs (a semantic property requiring inference) is not clearly specified, making exact reproduction of the refinement trigger difficult.

Cost comparison is incomplete: API cost is reported against Explorer ($0.13 vs $0.22 per trajectory), but not against OS-Genesis or Self-Instruct, so the end-to-end efficiency claim of the full pipeline (categorized exploration + dual refinement) is hard to assess.

Absolute performance remains modest (20.8 overall on WebArena vs 25.2 for GPT-4.1), and the ablation result that removing both refinements improves Shopping while degrading Maps suggests component interactions that are explained only post hoc and not fully understood.
Adaptations to the Explorer baseline (adding authentication support) are justified but complicate direct comparability with the original method's reported behavior.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: adapting web agents to new environments without human-annotated tasks, and the identified tension between task grounding and trajectory noise is clearly articulated and well-motivated.

The methodology is described at a level of detail that supports reproducibility: conflict-triggered refinement conditions (ExistsUI, MissingArgs, Stall) are formalized, trajectory refinement operations (Remove/Reorder/Drop/Keep) are specified, and all key prompts are included in the appendix.

The experimental design is reasonably comprehensive: two benchmarks (WebArena, Online-Mind2Web), multiple base models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B), several baselines re-implemented under the same GPT-4.1 teacher, a component-wise ablation (Table 5), data-scaling analysis, trajectory-completion/cost comparison against Explorer (Table 4), and quality ratings from three different judges (GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, Qwen3-30B) to mitigate single-judge bias.
The generalization result on Online-Mind2Web (training only on WebArena-derived synthetic data) is a meaningful test of whether the approach transfers rather than overfits to a fixed set of sites.

Honest reporting of negative/nuanced results, e.g., Explorer's poor performance is investigated and attributed to its algorithmic design rather than an implementation error, and the ablation reveals an interesting interaction where removing both refinements helps on Shopping but hurts on Maps.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in evaluation: GPT-4.1 is used both to refine tasks/trajectories and as a judge of their quality and as an execution agent, which could inflate quality scores for the proposed method even though additional judges (GPT-5.1, Qwen3-30B) are used; no human verification of refined trajectory validity is provided, which is important because trajectory refinement (reordering/removing steps) could produce trajectories inconsistent with actual environment states despite the claimed independence checks.

Evaluation sets are small and variability is not quantified: WebArena results use only 226 tasks (26 for CMS), and per-website scores show large swings (e.g., UI-TARS +OS-Genesis at 21.12 on Shopping vs. 0.0 on Maps); no confidence intervals, seeds, or significance tests are reported, making some claims (e.g., ablation differences of ~3-5%) hard to assess.

Gains over the strongest baselines are moderate and uneven: on UI-TARS, SynthAgent (17.26) is only modestly above Self-Instruct (13.33) and below OS-Genesis on Shopping (21.12 vs. 20.00), suggesting the advantage may depend on the base model; the paper does not analyze when/why the method helps less.

The 'fully synthetic, no test leakage' framing is somewhat undercut by details: the SFT upper bound uses the full 812 test tasks while synthetic methods are evaluated on a 226-task subset, and baseline adaptations (e.g., adding authentication support to Explorer) involve non-trivial reimplementation choices that could disadvantage baselines despite the authors' stated care.

The core recipe (categorized exploration plus refine-at-execution plus post-hoc trajectory cleanup) is an engineering combination of ideas from Explorer and OS-Genesis; the conceptual novelty beyond these close prior works is limited, and the paper would benefit from a sharper isolation of what is fundamentally new versus tuned.

Some claims lack direct evidence: diversity is scored by LLM judges and visualized via t-SNE rather than measured against executable coverage, and the synergy claim between task and trajectory refinement is supported mainly by one ablation cell (w/o TR&JR) with mixed per-site results.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper articulates a genuine tension in existing synthetic-data pipelines for web agents (task hallucination from insufficient grounding vs. trajectory noise from continuous task refinement), and the dual-refinement design directly addresses both sides of this tension rather than treating them as independent quality issues.

Comprehensive experimental design: evaluation spans an offline benchmark (WebArena, five websites) and an online benchmark (Online-Mind2Web, 136 live websites), with three independent LLM judges for data-quality assessment, which reduces dependence on a single evaluator and strengthens the robustness of the quality claims.

Useful supporting analyses: ablations (Table 5) isolate the contribution of categorized exploration, task refinement, and trajectory refinement; the Explorer-vs-SynthAgent comparison (Table 4) quantifies trajectory completion rates and API cost; the reorder head-to-head (Table 9) and edit-operation distribution (Table 8) provide evidence that trajectory refinement is conservative rather than fabricating quality; scaling behavior across data amounts (Figure 4) is examined.

Fair baseline treatment: all baselines use the same LLM (GPT-4.1), the same prompting/action space, and matched data budgets (500 task-trajectory pairs per website); the added authentication support for Explorer is disclosed and its failure mode is analyzed and attributed to the algorithmic design rather than an implementation error.

Reasonable reproducibility: full prompts for categorization, task generation, refinement, and trajectory refinement are provided in the appendix, implementation details (learning rate, batch size, context window, step budgets) are specified, and code is stated to be publicly available.

Practical significance: the fully synthetic setting (no human tasks, no test-task leakage) with consistent gains over both base models and prior synthesis methods is relevant to practitioners adapting agents to new sites, and the Online-Mind2Web result suggests the gains are not confined to the synthesis environments.
weaknesses: No variance reporting: all main results (Tables 1, 2, 5) appear to be from single training/evaluation runs, and WebArena evaluation is restricted to a 226-task subset. Several reported margins are modest (e.g., UI-TARS 17.26 vs. 14.60 for OS-Genesis; ablation deltas of ~3.5-5 points), so run-to-run variance and fine-tuning instability could affect the conclusions; multiple seeds or confidence intervals are needed.

The most striking baseline result (Explorer degrading the UI-TARS base model from 8.85 to 4.96) is unusual; although the authors provide a plausible explanation (continuous refinement causing budget overrun) and claim a faithful reimplementation, an independent-implementation check or a variant of Explorer with a tighter refinement policy would make the comparison more convincing.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge for the core data-quality claims (Tables 3, 10, 11): although three judges are used and rankings are consistent, the judges share known biases with the generation model (GPT-4.1/GPT-5.1 family), and no human verification of a sample of tasks/trajectories is reported to anchor the judge scores.

The synthesis pipeline depends entirely on a strong closed-source model (GPT-4.1); a cost analysis is given only for trajectory collection, and there is no discussion of how the approach degrades with weaker synthesis models or how total per-website synthesis cost compares to alternatives.

Some framing overstates novelty: Explorer also performs refinement during collection and OS-Genesis also grounds tasks in environment interactions; the contribution is best characterized as a careful redesign of the refinement trigger (conflict-based vs. continuous) plus categorized exploration, which is incremental even if effective.

Presentation issues: appendix cross-references are inconsistent (e.g., Section A.6-A.9 reference 'Table 7/8/9' for prompts while the actual prompt tables are numbered differently), Figure 1's abstract-level framing oversimplifies prior work, and the claim that trajectory refinement 'without re-interacting with the environment' preserves validity is asserted rather than directly verified beyond the reorder study.
The t-SNE diversity analysis (Figure 3) is qualitative; embedding-based diversity claims would benefit from a quantitative measure, and the diversity scores in Table 3 are again judge-dependent.
